entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

When an event lands that the user would want to act on now — an error appeared, the status they were waiting on flipped — send a PushNotification. Not every event is worth a push; the ones that change what they'd do next are.

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

"""Measures the firmware's size, RAM and speed, and gates them (checks
C-PERF and C-PERF-PROBES; R-PERF-1 to R-PERF-5).

  perf.py check --build DIR --out DIR [--base-ref REF] [--records-ref REF]
                [--require-records]
      Measures DIR/app.bin (a tools/build.sh output), finds the latest
      record of a main commit (the first-parent history of --base-ref,
      default origin/main, on --records-ref, default origin/records),
      measures that record's own app.bin the same way, and applies the
      gates. Writes OUT/perf.json. Exit status 1 if a gate failed.
  perf.py probes --build DIR --out DIR
      Builds the firmware with SB_PROBE_SLOW, SB_PROBE_BIG and (since
      M4b) SB_PROBE_LOADED (firmware/src/probe.c), measures each, and
      checks that the gates fail each one for its own reason, measured
      against DIR/app.bin: the slower build its speed and its steady-state
      budget, the bigger build each size budget and its startup budget,
      the loaded build its loaded speed and loaded budget, with the
      unmodified build's measurements as those budgets. Builds it also with SB_PROBE_STACK
      and checks the stack's high-water mark shows at least the 1 KiB that
      build is known to use.
      Exit status 1 if any gate did not fail as it should.
  perf.py history --record REPORT.json --csv FILE [--measures FILE]
      Appends the record's line to perf-history.csv (records workflow),
      and since M4b its rows to perf-measures.csv, one per measure. Never
      rewrites either file; a commit (and measure) that already has a
      line is left.
  perf.py summary --record REPORT.json

-### 2026-10-24 M7: flash storage
-- Facts: HW-5 (the code window shows the chip from offset `0x4000` in
-  fwtest), HW-47 (SPI0, the chip select, the commands); and SR-9's answer,
-  HW-76 to HW-82 (#97, read from its branch before it merged): the part
-  (the P25Q80H, if the FM-1 carries it: Q-21), its times and endurance,
-  its command rules, nothing from the window while the flash is busy,
-  the FM-1's flash layout, the window encrypted and cached on the chip,
-  fwtest 0.5.0's chip; HARNESS.md's `--flash`, `--flash-out` and its
-  known gap around an unused volatile read. PROVENANCE P-54.
-- Sources: our own design. No other firmware's store, no file system's
-  or EEPROM-emulation library's source, was looked at for it.
-#### Nothing runs from the window
-On the chip the code window is the flash itself, and while an erase or a
-program is in progress nothing may be read through it, on either core
-(HW-79); a 4 KiB erase takes up to 12 ms, longer than a half of the audio
-buffer lasts. So the firmware no longer reads the window once main runs
-(the first of HW-79's ways to keep the audio going): the
-linker places every instruction and constant in RAM (`.data`, from
-`__ram_code_start` to `__ram_code_end`), and the start-up copy that
-already copied the initial data copies them too (24 KiB, about 63 us more
-at the start). Only `_start`, the stack fill and `sb_start` run from the
-window (`.boot.text`, 120 bytes). Core 1, the interrupt handlers and the
-vector table's addresses are all RAM addresses. The store reads the chip
-through SPI0's read command, never through the window, as HW-81 asks
-(the window is encrypted and cached on the chip). The wipe test build
-proves the rest:
-it erases its own image once main runs, and the heaviest load with saves
-then plays on with no underrun and no fault. `tools/build.sh` still
-counts all of it as code, and `ram_code` says how much runs from RAM;
-since it takes RAM, `tools/perf.py` counts it in static RAM too.
-#### The store
-A ring of 18 sectors of 4 KiB, chip offsets `0xEA000` to `0xFBFFF`
-(docs/STORE-FORMAT.md has the bytes). The region is the stock layout's
-user patch region (HW-80): out of the boot area, the Bluetooth sector
-and the per-unit last sector. A first draft used the chip's last 64 KiB,
-which HW-80 showed includes that last sector; the move was one define.
-Where our own image sits on the chip is M9's to settle (Q-24), so the
-region stays one definition. The choices:
-- **Append only, CRC on everything.** A record is never changed once
-  written, so a power cut can only leave the newest record incomplete;
-  its CRC-32 fails and the copy before it is read. No commit bit, no
-  second write to the same bytes: that keeps the store right whatever a
-  program cut short leaves in the bits, and whatever the chip does when a
-  program meets bits that are not erased.
-- **Read whole sectors, in 16-byte steps.** A torn record can leave erased
-  blocks inside it, so an erased block is no sign that a sector's records
-  have ended; the reader goes on to the sector's end, and the head takes
-  new records only after its last byte that is not erased. A torn record
-  therefore never closes the head. (An earlier draft closed it, and the
-  sweep's design showed the trap: a cut during a compaction would leave a
-  closed head with live records still in the sector after it, and every
-  save after it refused.)
-- **The ring and its compaction.** The sector after the head holds nothing
-  live, always: when the head is full, that sector is erased and becomes
-  the head, and the live records of the sector after it are copied in.
-  All the live records together (16 patches, the selection, the
-  settings, a reset) take 2 160 bytes, so they always fit one sector with
-  room to spare; `tests/test_store.py` checks it. A cut during a
-  compaction leaves the originals where they were; the next save finishes
-  the copying first.
-- **Reset is a record.** The factory reset writes one record that voids
-  every older one, so it is as safe against a cut as any save, and wears
-  nothing. A reset is always copied forward.
-- **The part's rules** (HW-78): a write enable before every erase and
-  program, a page program never past its page, the end of each waited for
-  on the status register's WIP bit, never by a delay. Start-up reads the
-  JEDEC ID, and a part other than the P25Q80H (HW-76) is read but never
-  written (`STORE_ERR_PART`), since its rules and times are not known.
-  SPI0's sending side never reads `BUF`, which also keeps clear of fwtest
-  0.5.0's gap around an unused volatile read (HARNESS.md).
-- **Start-up** reads the ID, 18 headers and every valid sector: under a
-  millisecond for an empty store, about 4.5 ms for a full one (72 KiB
-  through SPI0 in fwtest, where a byte takes no time of its own, HW-82;
-  on the chip SPI0's clock sets it).
-- **Main does it all.** The engine never waits: it takes the panel's save
-  in its block callback, stores the patch in RAM at once, and adds one to
-  that slot's save count; main's loop writes every slot whose count moved
-  (and none a later reset voided), then the reset. The selection and the
-  settings are compared once a second. While main waits for the flash the
-  interrupts stay on, so the audio, the tick, the scan and core 1 go on;
-  the screen waits.
-#### Wear
-- **Limits by kind** (`STORE_SETTLE_S`, R-STORE-8): the selection and the
-  settings are written only when they changed, at most once every 2 s; a
-  patch only when the player saves it; a reset only when asked. Under
-  PRESETS turned four times a second for 6 s, the selection was written 4
-  times (wear).
-- **Spread:** every sector is erased in turn (the ring), so each takes one
-  erase in 18. The model writes 6 000 random saves with erase counts
-  within one of each other (`tests/test_store.py`).
-- **Lifetime:** the P25Q80H takes 100 000 erase cycles a sector (HW-77).
-  A sector has 1 920 bytes for new records after the largest compaction,
-  so the region takes 18 x 1 920 x 100 000 bytes of records: the
-  selection and the settings both changing every 2 s without a break
-  (96 bytes in 2 s) last about 2.3 years; a patch saved every 10 s
-  without a break, about 8.6 years. Real use is a small part of either.
-#### The panel (minimal; the full UI is M8)
-- **Save:** hold SAVE and press one of the 16 leftmost keys (KEY1 to
-  KEY16, lower and raised keys counted left to right, HW-37): the patch
-  playing now is
-  saved to that user slot, with the algorithm ALGORITHM chose and the
-  mode SEL with MONO or POLY chose; no note plays while SAVE is held. The
-  screen's event line says "saved to slot n" (or "SAVE FAILED, slot n").
-  KNOB1 to KNOB4 stay offsets over the patch, as they are over every
-  patch, and are not saved, so a saved patch never takes them twice.
-  The program stays as it was.
-- **Programs:** PRESETS and program changes reach the test patches (0 to
-  8), then the user slots that hold a patch (9 to 24). With no user
-  slots, PRESETS turns as before.
-- **Factory defaults:** hold SAVE and HOME together for 2 s: every user
-  slot empty, the settings' defaults, the first program; the event line
-  says "factory defaults". Held less, nothing happens.
-- **Kept without asking:** the selection and the settings, once they have
-  stayed changed for 2 s (above).
-#### How it is tested (R-STORE-1 to R-STORE-9)
-`tools/store_suite.py`, run by `tools/fw-suite.py` after the suite, since
-its runs need the flash another run left. `tools/store.py` reads every
-image the way the firmware does, and where a case starts from an image it
-made, its model also predicts the image the firmware leaves, command for
-command; the two are compared byte for byte. The sweep's save takes a new
-head, erases it and copies 17 live records (28 commands); the cut test
-build stops after each command and part way through each page program
-(109 cuts), and the model adds programs with half their bits cleared and
-erases half done (29 images). Every image holds the old patch or the new
-and nothing else changed, and the shipping image starts from each one,
-finds what `tools/store.py` finds, and saves again. The busy test build
-makes each erase take 12 ms and each page program 3 ms, the part's
-longest (HW-77; an earlier run at 400 ms an erase passed too); three
-saves under the heaviest panel load still leave no underrun and every
-tick within 2 time base ticks.
-#### Open (SR-9's open questions)
-- **Q-21, the part:** read on a unit; the ID check above refuses to write
-  to any other until its datasheet is read.
-- **Q-22, SPI0 on the chip:** how the window's controller hands the flash
-  to SPI0 and back, SPI0's clock and mode, and the chip select (fwtest
-  takes PD0; on the chip it may be another pin). The driver writes only
-  HW-47's bits; what the chip needs goes in `store_init` and the select
-  functions. Core 1 already runs from RAM, so it needn't be stopped.
-- **Q-23, write protection:** if a unit's protect bits are set, a write
-  reads back wrong and the save is reported failed (never silently lost).
-- **Q-24, updates:** whether an update rewrites the user region decides
-  whether saved patches survive one (M9).

-# M8 proposal: from engine to instrument
-A proposal for the owner to review, written at the end of M7. Nothing
-here is built yet. It uses only what the firmware and the panel already
-offer, and facts already in HARDWARE-SPEC.md. Decisions wanted are at
-the end.
-## What we start from
-- **Panel** (HW-36): a 240 x 240 colour screen; eight knobs (MASTER, a
-  pot; SELECT, PRESETS, ALGORITHM and KNOB1 to KNOB4, encoders with
-  detents); 14 buttons (OCT-, OCT+, FX, SEL, ENV, LFO, EDIT, GLO, HOME,
-  SAVE, ARP, SEQ, PLAY/STOP, REC), each with an LED; 27 keys, each with an
-  LED, ten raised keys carrying second labels: OP1 to OP6, PIT, GLO,
-  MONO, POLY.
-- **Engine** (M5 to M7): six operators, ten algorithms, 16 voices on two
-  cores, a pitch envelope, mono with glide, MIDI in and out, 9 test
-  patches, 16 user slots kept in flash.
-- **Today's controls:** PRESETS picks a program, ALGORITHM the algorithm,
-  KNOB1 to KNOB4 are pitch, glide, modulation depth and feedback; SEL
-  with MONO or POLY sets the mode; SAVE with a key saves.
-## Four rules
-1. **One screen at a time; HOME always goes back** to the patch view.
-2. **The bottom strip names what KNOB1 to KNOB4 do** on every screen,
-   with their values, so the knobs are never a guess.
-3. **Some knobs never change meaning:** MASTER is volume, PRESETS the
-   program, OCT- and OCT+ the octave, everywhere.
-4. **The screen shows the sound,** not only numbers: the algorithm
-   drawn with each operator's level moving as it plays, and a spectrum
-   of what comes out.
-## The screens
-### Patch view (HOME)
-| 012  GLASS BELL           POLY  O+0  |
-|  1>2 3>4   spectrum, live            |
-| BRIGHT  COLOR   SHAPE   MOTION       |
-The program and its name, the mode and octave; a small picture of the
-algorithm; the live spectrum. KNOB1 to KNOB4 are the four macros
-(below). ALGORITHM changes the algorithm, as now.
-### Operator and algorithm view (EDIT)
-| ALG 5            OP3 selected        |
-|   ##     #       ## = level now      |
-|  [3]==>[4]   (selected: double line) |
-| RATIO   LEVEL   DETUNE  VELO         |
-The algorithm drawn as boxes and arrows, carriers at the bottom. Under
-each box a bar shows that operator's level now (the loudest voice), so
-you see a modulator decay while the note sounds. SEL with OP1 to OP6
-picks the operator, whose key LED stays lit; KNOB1 to KNOB4 edit it.
-SELECT steps through the operator's other pages (mode and fixed
-frequency; the envelope's levels).
-### Envelope view (ENV)
-| ENV  OP3                  stage: D1  |
-| ATTACK  DECAY1  DECAY2  RELEASE      |
-The selected operator's envelope drawn to scale (time codes are
-logarithmic, so the drawing is too), and a dot where the last note is
-now. SELECT switches the knobs to the three levels. SEL with PIT shows
-the pitch envelope instead; SEL with GLO, the glide.
-### Settings (GLO)
-| SETTINGS                             |
-| > MIDI in channel     omni           |
-|   MIDI out channel    1              |
-|   Thru                off            |
-|   Local control       on             |
-|   Bend range          2              |
-|   Knobs               macros         |
-|   Store               5/16 used      |
-|   Factory reset       hold SAVE      |
-| SELECT: row    KNOB1: change         |
-Every setting in `struct midi_settings`, plus the knobs' mode (macros or
-the M5 controls) and the store's state. Changes are kept as M7 keeps
-them (2 s after the last change).
-### Save (SAVE)
-| SAVE  GLASS BELL  to slot:           |
-| SELECT: slot  SAVE: write  HOME: no  |
-M7's shortcut (SAVE held with a key) stays; the screen adds names, a
-slot picker and a confirmation before overwriting a slot in use.
-## The controls
-| Control | Everywhere | Patch | EDIT | ENV | Settings |
-| MASTER | volume | | | | |
-| PRESETS | program | | | | |
-| ALGORITHM | | algorithm | algorithm | | |
-| SELECT | | | operator page | rates / levels | row |
-| KNOB1-4 | | macros | operator | stage times | value (KNOB1) |

-SEL is the shift key: held, the raised keys do what their second label
-says and play no note. Keys without SEL always play. LEDs: the screen's
-button lit; the selected operator's key at half brightness; held keys
-fully lit, as now.
-## The four macros (KNOB1 to KNOB4 in the patch view)
-Each macro moves several of the patch's values at once, as an offset
-over the stored patch (as KNOB1 to KNOB4 do today), so turning it back
-returns the patch exactly. Each is sent and received as one MIDI
-controller (16 to 19, as now).
-- **BRIGHT** (brightness): every modulator's level up or down together,
-  so the index and the upper partials rise or fall. Today's KNOB3,
-  renamed.
-- **COLOR** (harmonic to metallic): the modulators' ratios move from
-  their whole-number values towards inharmonic ones (a fixed table of
-  targets per ratio, so the sweep is the same on every patch), and
-  feedback rises a little at the metallic end.
-- **SHAPE** (pluck to pad): the carriers' envelopes. At one end a fast
-  attack, a short decay and little sustain; at the other a slow attack,
-  full sustain and a long release. The middle is the patch as stored.
-- **MOTION:** vibrato depth, plus a small spread of detune across the
-  carriers, so a held note moves and widens.

-setting ("Knobs: direct"), for tests and for players who want them.

-- **How many:** 64 presets in 8 categories of 8: keys, bass, bells and
-  mallets, brass and winds, pads, leads, plucks and strings, percussion
-  and effects. They sit in the image, after the 9 test patches; the 16
-  user slots stay as M7 made them.
-- **How they are made:** written from scratch in `tools/fm_patch.py`,
-  as the test patches are: ratios, levels and envelopes chosen by ear
-  and by reasoning (a bell's inharmonic ratios, a bass's short
-  modulator decay), each with a line saying what it is for. Never
-  derived from anyone's factory sounds: no voice banks or SysEx dumps are
-  opened, converted or compared, and no names are borrowed. Each preset's
-  history is its commits.

-  - valid by `fm_patch.problems()`, and all 16 voices sounding within
-    the loaded budget;
-  - a reference note: no clipping, no DC, no click at note on or off,

-  - its category's shape: a bass has most of its energy below 300 Hz, a
-    pad no attack faster than 50 ms, a pluck decays by 30 dB within 2 s;
-  - a golden WAV of the reference note, so any change shows;

+- Facts: HW-5 (the code window shows the chip from offset `0x4000` in

+- Sources: our own design. No other firmware's store, no file system's
+  or EEPROM-emulation library's source, was looked at for it.
+#### Nothing runs from the window
+On the chip the code window is the flash itself, and while an erase or a
+program is in progress nothing may be read through it, on either core
+(HW-79); a 4 KiB erase takes up to 12 ms, longer than a half of the audio
+buffer lasts. So the firmware no longer reads the window once main runs
+(the first of HW-79's ways to keep the audio going): the
+linker places every instruction and constant in RAM (`.data`, from
+`__ram_code_start` to `__ram_code_end`), and the start-up copy that
+already copied the initial data copies them too (24 KiB, about 63 us more
+at the start). Only `_start`, the stack fill and `sb_start` run from the
+window (`.boot.text`, 120 bytes). Core 1, the interrupt handlers and the
+vector table's addresses are all RAM addresses. The store reads the chip
+through SPI0's read command, never through the window, as HW-81 asks
+(the window is encrypted and cached on the chip). The wipe test build
+proves the rest:
+it erases its own image once main runs, and the heaviest load with saves
+then plays on with no underrun and no fault. `tools/build.sh` still
+counts all of it as code, and `ram_code` says how much runs from RAM;
+since it takes RAM, `tools/perf.py` counts it in static RAM too.
+#### The store
+A ring of 18 sectors of 4 KiB, chip offsets `0xEA000` to `0xFBFFF`
+(docs/STORE-FORMAT.md has the bytes). The region is the stock layout's
+user patch region (HW-80): out of the boot area, the Bluetooth sector
+and the per-unit last sector. A first draft used the chip's last 64 KiB,
+which HW-80 showed includes that last sector; the move was one define.
+Where our own image sits on the chip is M9's to settle (Q-24), so the
+region stays one definition. The choices:
+- **Append only, CRC on everything.** A record is never changed once
+  written, so a power cut can only leave the newest record incomplete;
+  its CRC-32 fails and the copy before it is read. No commit bit, no
+  second write to the same bytes: that keeps the store right whatever a
+  program cut short leaves in the bits, and whatever the chip does when a
+  program meets bits that are not erased.
+- **Read whole sectors, in 16-byte steps.** A torn record can leave erased
+  blocks inside it, so an erased block is no sign that a sector's records
+  have ended; the reader goes on to the sector's end, and the head takes
+  new records only after its last byte that is not erased. A torn record
+  therefore never closes the head. (An earlier draft closed it, and the
+  sweep's design showed the trap: a cut during a compaction would leave a
+  closed head with live records still in the sector after it, and every
+  save after it refused.)
+- **The ring and its compaction.** The sector after the head holds nothing
+  live, always: when the head is full, that sector is erased and becomes
+  the head, and the live records of the sector after it are copied in.
+  All the live records together (16 patches, the selection, the
+  settings, a reset) take 2 160 bytes, so they always fit one sector with
+  room to spare; `tests/test_store.py` checks it. A cut during a
+  compaction leaves the originals where they were; the next save finishes
+  the copying first.
+- **Reset is a record.** The factory reset writes one record that voids
+  every older one, so it is as safe against a cut as any save, and wears
+  nothing. A reset is always copied forward.
+- **The part's rules** (HW-78): a write enable before every erase and
+  program, a page program never past its page, the end of each waited for
+  on the status register's WIP bit, never by a delay. Start-up reads the
+  JEDEC ID, and a part other than the P25Q80H (HW-76) is read but never
+  written (`STORE_ERR_PART`), since its rules and times are not known.
+  SPI0's sending side never reads `BUF`, which also keeps clear of fwtest
+  0.5.0's gap around an unused volatile read (HARNESS.md).
+- **Start-up** reads the ID, 18 headers and every valid sector: under a
+  millisecond for an empty store, about 4.5 ms for a full one (72 KiB
+  through SPI0 in fwtest, where a byte takes no time of its own, HW-82;
+  on the chip SPI0's clock sets it).
+- **Main does it all.** The engine never waits: it takes the panel's save
+  in its block callback, stores the patch in RAM at once, and adds one to
+  that slot's save count; main's loop writes every slot whose count moved
+  (and none a later reset voided), then the reset. The selection and the
+  settings are compared once a second. While main waits for the flash the
+  interrupts stay on, so the audio, the tick, the scan and core 1 go on;
+  the screen waits.
+#### Wear
+- **Limits by kind** (`STORE_SETTLE_S`, R-STORE-8): the selection and the
+  settings are written only when they changed, at most once every 2 s; a
+  patch only when the player saves it; a reset only when asked. Under
+  PRESETS turned four times a second for 6 s, the selection was written 4
+  times (wear).
+- **Spread:** every sector is erased in turn (the ring), so each takes one
+  erase in 18. The model writes 6 000 random saves with erase counts
+  within one of each other (`tests/test_store.py`).
+- **Lifetime:** the P25Q80H takes 100 000 erase cycles a sector (HW-77).
+  A sector has 1 920 bytes for new records after the largest compaction,
+  so the region takes 18 x 1 920 x 100 000 bytes of records: the
+  selection and the settings both changing every 2 s without a break
+  (96 bytes in 2 s) last about 2.3 years; a patch saved every 10 s
+  without a break, about 8.6 years. Real use is a small part of either.
+#### The panel (minimal; the full UI is M8)
+- **Save:** hold SAVE and press one of the 16 leftmost keys (KEY1 to
+  KEY16, lower and raised keys counted left to right, HW-37): the patch
+  playing now is
+  saved to that user slot, with the algorithm ALGORITHM chose and the
+  mode SEL with MONO or POLY chose; no note plays while SAVE is held. The
+  screen's event line says "saved to slot n" (or "SAVE FAILED, slot n").
+  KNOB1 to KNOB4 stay offsets over the patch, as they are over every
+  patch, and are not saved, so a saved patch never takes them twice.
+  The program stays as it was.
+- **Programs:** PRESETS and program changes reach the test patches (0 to
+  8), then the user slots that hold a patch (9 to 24). With no user
+  slots, PRESETS turns as before.
+- **Factory defaults:** hold SAVE and HOME together for 2 s: every user
+  slot empty, the settings' defaults, the first program; the event line
+  says "factory defaults". Held less, nothing happens.
+- **Kept without asking:** the selection and the settings, once they have
+  stayed changed for 2 s (above).
+#### How it is tested (R-STORE-1 to R-STORE-9)
+`tools/store_suite.py`, run by `tools/fw-suite.py` after the suite, since
+its runs need the flash another run left. `tools/store.py` reads every
+image the way the firmware does, and where a case starts from an image it
+made, its model also predicts the image the firmware leaves, command for
+command; the two are compared byte for byte. The sweep's save takes a new
+head, erases it and copies 17 live records (28 commands); the cut test
+build stops after each command and part way through each page program
+(109 cuts), and the model adds programs with half their bits cleared and
+erases half done (29 images). Every image holds the old patch or the new
+and nothing else changed, and the shipping image starts from each one,
+finds what `tools/store.py` finds, and saves again. The busy test build
+makes each erase take 12 ms and each page program 3 ms, the part's
+longest (HW-77; an earlier run at 400 ms an erase passed too); three
+saves under the heaviest panel load still leave no underrun and every
+tick within 2 time base ticks.
+#### Open (SR-9's open questions)
+- **Q-21, the part:** read on a unit; the ID check above refuses to write

+- **Q-22, SPI0 on the chip:** how the window's controller hands the flash
+  to SPI0 and back, SPI0's clock and mode, and the chip select (fwtest

+- **Q-23, write protection:** if a unit's protect bits are set, a write
+  reads back wrong and the save is reported failed (never silently lost).
+- **Q-24, updates:** whether an update rewrites the user region decides

+# M8 proposal: from engine to instrument
+A proposal for the owner to review, written at the end of M7. Nothing
+here is built yet. It uses only what the firmware and the panel already
+offer, and facts already in HARDWARE-SPEC.md. Decisions wanted are at
+the end.
+## What we start from
+- **Panel** (HW-36): a 240 x 240 colour screen; eight knobs (MASTER, a
+  pot; SELECT, PRESETS, ALGORITHM and KNOB1 to KNOB4, encoders with
+  detents); 14 buttons (OCT-, OCT+, FX, SEL, ENV, LFO, EDIT, GLO, HOME,
+  SAVE, ARP, SEQ, PLAY/STOP, REC), each with an LED; 27 keys, each with an
+  LED, ten raised keys carrying second labels: OP1 to OP6, PIT, GLO,
+  MONO, POLY.
+- **Engine** (M5 to M7): six operators, ten algorithms, 16 voices on two
+  cores, a pitch envelope, mono with glide, MIDI in and out, 9 test
+  patches, 16 user slots kept in flash.
+- **Today's controls:** PRESETS picks a program, ALGORITHM the algorithm,
+  KNOB1 to KNOB4 are pitch, glide, modulation depth and feedback; SEL
+  with MONO or POLY sets the mode; SAVE with a key saves.
+## Four rules
+1. **One screen at a time; HOME always goes back** to the patch view.
+2. **The bottom strip names what KNOB1 to KNOB4 do** on every screen,
+   with their values, so the knobs are never a guess.
+3. **Some knobs never change meaning:** MASTER is volume, PRESETS the
+   program, OCT- and OCT+ the octave, everywhere.
+4. **The screen shows the sound,** not only numbers: the algorithm
+   drawn with each operator's level moving as it plays, and a spectrum
+   of what comes out.

+## The four macros (KNOB1 to KNOB4 in the patch view)
+Each macro moves several of the patch's values at once, as an offset
+over the stored patch (as KNOB1 to KNOB4 do today), so turning it back
+returns the patch exactly. Each is sent and received as one MIDI
+controller (16 to 19, as now).
+- **BRIGHT** (brightness): every modulator's level up or down together,
+  so the index and the upper partials rise or fall. Today's KNOB3,
+  renamed.
+- **COLOR** (harmonic to metallic): the modulators' ratios move from
+  their whole-number values towards inharmonic ones (a fixed table of
+  targets per ratio, so the sweep is the same on every patch), and
+  feedback rises a little at the metallic end.
+- **SHAPE** (pluck to pad): the carriers' envelopes. At one end a fast
+  attack, a short decay and little sustain; at the other a slow attack,
+  full sustain and a long release. The middle is the patch as stored.
+- **MOTION:** vibrato depth, plus a small spread of detune across the
+  carriers, so a held note moves and widens.

+setting ("Knobs: direct"), for tests and for players who want them.
+## Presets: a bank of our own
+- **How many:** 64 presets in 8 categories of 8: keys, bass, bells and
+  mallets, brass and winds, pads, leads, plucks and strings, percussion
+  and effects. They sit in the image, after the 9 test patches; the 16
+  user slots stay as M7 made them.
+- **How they are made:** written from scratch in `tools/fm_patch.py`,
+  as the test patches are: ratios, levels and envelopes chosen by ear
+  and by reasoning (a bell's inharmonic ratios, a bass's short
+  modulator decay), each with a line saying what it is for. Never
+  derived from anyone's factory sounds: no voice banks or SysEx dumps are
+  opened, converted or compared, and no names are borrowed. Each preset's
+  history is its commits.
+- **How they are tested,** each one in fwtest, by a tool of our own:
+  - valid by `fm_patch.problems()`, and all 16 voices sounding within
+    the loaded budget;
+  - a reference note: no clipping, no DC, no click at note on or off,
+    loudness within 3 dB of a target, so the bank plays at one level;
+  - its category's shape: a bass has most of its energy below 300 Hz, a
+    pad no attack faster than 50 ms, a pluck decays by 30 dB within 2 s;
+  - a golden WAV of the reference note, so any change shows;
+  - and the owner listens before the bank is merged.
+## Costs
+From M5 to M7's measurements (fwtest): a block is 64 frames, 1.451 ms,
+about 348 000 core cycles at 240 MHz. Under the heaviest input, core 0
+spends about 110 000 instructions a block (32%), core 1 about 22%, and
+the screen may take at most 4 352 time base ticks a block, about 43 500
+instructions (12.5%). On the chip the panel's bus needs at least 60.8 ms
+for a whole frame (DESIGN-NOTES, M2), so live views redraw small regions,
+never the whole screen.
+| Live view | Core 0, each update | At 30 updates a second | Panel bus, at 30 a second |
+| Spectrum: 256-point real FFT of the output, 64 bars, 240 x 40 pixels | about 15 000 instructions (FFT with the float unit, window, magnitudes) | about 650 a block, 0.2% | 10.1 ms an update: 30% |
+| Algorithm: 6 level bars of 30 x 20 pixels | about 10 000 | about 430 a block, 0.1% | 3.8 ms an update: 11% |
+| Envelope dot | under 2 000 | under 100 a block | under 1% |

+update fits in one block's drawing budget. The bus is the limit: both
+live views at 30 updates a second take about 41% of it (at 20, about

+updates a second on the patch view's spectrum alone, 20 when the
+algorithm's bars show too. RAM: about 2 KiB for the FFT's buffers
+(the output's last 256 samples, copied by the engine each block). The
+engine adds one small record for the views: each operator's loudest
+level, written once a block. Nothing moves to core 1.

+# The store's format, version 1
+The firmware keeps its user patches, the patch selection and the settings
+in a store of our own design (M7; `firmware/src/store.c`, and
+docs/DESIGN-NOTES.md, M7, for why it is built this way). This is its
+layout on the flash chip. `tools/store.py` reads and writes the same
+format, and `tests/test_store.py` checks that its constants are the
+firmware's. Numbers are little-endian.
+## The region
+Chip offsets `0xEA000` to `0xFBFFF`, the stock layout's user patch
+region (HW-80): 18 sectors of 4 KiB, used as a ring. Where it sits is one
+definition (`STORE_BASE` and `STORE_SIZE` in `store.h`), since where our
+own image sits on the chip is M9's; `firmware/app.ld` keeps the image
+clear of it. The firmware reads and writes the region only through
+SPI0's flash commands (HW-47, HW-78), never through the code window
+## A sector
+Each sector starts with a 16-byte header:
+| Offset | Bytes | Field |
+| 4 | 4 | sequence number: one more than the sector that was the head before it |
+| 8 | 1 | format: 1 |
+| 12 | 4 | CRC-32 of bytes 0 to 11 |
+A sector whose header is not valid holds nothing. The valid sector with
+the highest sequence number is the **head**, the one that takes new
+records.
+## A record
+Records start on a 16-byte boundary after the sector's header:
+| Offset | Bytes | Field |
+| 0 | 1 | magic 0xA5 |
+| 1 | 1 | kind (below) |
+| 2 | 1 | id: the user slot, 0 to 15, for a patch; 0 otherwise |
+| 3 | 1 | the payload's version |
+| 4 | 2 | the payload's length, at most 112 |
+| 8 | 4 | sequence number: one more than the record written before it |
+| 12 | length | the payload |
+| 12 + length | 4 | CRC-32 of the header and the payload |
+The bytes after the CRC, up to the next 16-byte boundary, are left erased.
+The CRC-32 is the common one (reflected, polynomial 0xEDB88320, all ones in
+and out: zlib's).
+| Kind | What | Payload, its version |
+| 1 | a user slot's patch | the 112-byte patch (docs/PATCH-FORMAT.md), version 1 |
+| 2 | the patch selection | 4 bytes: the program (0 to 8 the test patches, 9 to 24 the user slots), then 0, 0, 0; version 1 |

+| 3 | the settings | `struct midi_settings` (`firmware/src/midi.h`): version 2, 40 bytes; version 1 (M6a's), 36 bytes, is read as version 2 with version 2's defaults for the out channel (1), thru (off) and local control (on) |
+| 4 | a reset | none; version 0. Every record older than it is void |
+## Reading
+Every valid sector is read whole, in 16-byte steps from offset 16. A block
+that is erased is passed over; a block that is neither erased nor the
+start of a valid record (its magic, a length that fits, its CRC) is
+passed over too and counted. Of the records with the same kind and id,
+the one with the highest sequence number counts; then every record older
+than the newest reset is void. A record of a kind or id the reader does
+not know is counted and otherwise ignored, and never copied forward.
+## Writing
+A record is appended in the head after its last byte that is not erased,
+programmed in one go (a page program for each 256-byte page it touches),
+and read back. Nothing written is ever written again: a record replaces
+an older one only by being newer.
+When the head has no room, the next sector in the ring becomes the head:
+it is erased, and its header written with the next sequence number. Then
+every record still live in the sector after the new head (the oldest) is
+copied into the new head, with a new sequence number, so that sector holds
+nothing live by the time the ring comes round to erase it. If a sector
+can't be freed without losing a live record, the write is refused and
+nothing is written.
+## Versions
+Version 1 is the first (M7). A later format changes the sector header's
+format byte, and says here what changed; a payload's own version changes
+when its layout does, and the reader migrates what it knows.

**What:** M7, flash storage. User patches, the patch selection and the settings are kept in flash, safe against a power cut at any instant, and saving never disturbs the audio.
- **Nothing runs from the code window after start-up.** Every instruction and constant is copied to RAM; only the boot code stays in the window.
- **The store** (`firmware/src/store.c`, `docs/STORE-FORMAT.md`), our own design:
  - a ring of 18 sectors in the stock layout's user region, `0xEA000`–`0xFBFFF`;
  - append-only records, each with a CRC-32; the newest valid copy wins;
  - compaction into a fresh sector, and a reset record;
  - read and written over SPI0 only; a part with an unknown JEDEC ID is never written.
- **What it keeps** (`firmware/src/saving.c`):
  - 16 user slots;
  - the selection, and `struct midi_settings` (version 1 is migrated to version 2), each written 2 s after it changes, at most once in 2 s.
- **Panel (minimal, until M8):**
  - SAVE held with one of the 16 leftmost keys saves the patch playing now to that slot; PRESETS then reaches the slot after the test patches;
  - SAVE and HOME held for 2 s restore the factory defaults;
  - the event line on the screen says what happened.
- **Tests** (`tools/store_suite.py`, run by the fw suite; `tools/store.py`, the format's reader and model; `tests/test_store.py`).
- **Docs:** DESIGN-NOTES.md (M7), STORE-FORMAT.md, R-STORE-1 to R-STORE-9, PROVENANCE P-54, PLAN.md (M7 done, M8 next).

**Why:** M7 (R-STORE-1 to R-STORE-9).

**How:** the design and what was rejected are in DESIGN-NOTES.md, M7. In short:
- **Audio while the flash is busy.** HW-79 says nothing may be read through the window then, so everything runs from RAM and the interrupts stay on.
- **Power cuts.** Records are append-only and each carries a CRC, so a cut can only leave the newest record torn; the copy before it is then read.
- **Torn records.** Each sector is read whole, in 16-byte steps. A torn record never closes the head sector; an earlier draft did, and a cut during a compaction could then wedge the store.
- **No save is lost.** Each slot has its own save count, plus a reset epoch, so two saves before main serves them both reach the flash.

**Result:** local `tools/record.py run`: every check passes except two that fail only locally:
- C-REUSE: the `reuse` tool isn't installed on this Mac; every new file has an SPDX header.
- C-RECORD-PRIVATE: the local logs carry this Mac's paths and are withheld.

The store's nine cases (fwtest 0.5.0):

| Case | What it showed |
|---|---|
| persist | a save, a selection and a setting are there at the next start; the slot plays as program 9 |
| sweep | a save that takes a new sector, erases it and copies 17 live records (28 flash commands): cut after each command and part way through each page program (109 cuts), plus 29 torn images from the model (bits half cleared, erases half done). Every image is the model's exactly, with the old patch or the new and nothing else changed; every start from one agrees with `tools/store.py` and saves again |
| reset | held 2.4 s it empties the store; held 1 s it does nothing |
| corrupt | a damaged record, garbage and an unknown kind are ignored, and the older copy is read |
| full | with no sector freeable, the save is refused and nothing is written |
| wear | 36 saves erase sectors in ring order; the selection is written 4 times in 6 s of turns |
| migrate | version 1 settings are taken as version 2 |
| busy | 3 saves under the heaviest load with the part's longest times (12 ms an erase, 3 ms a page program; longest save 94.6 ms): 0 underruns, every tick within 2 time-base ticks |
| wipe | the firmware erases its own image, then plays on under load with saves: 0 underruns |

Performance against the M7 budgets (#98):
- steady state 1 877.1 instructions a block, +0.7%;
- loaded 107 136.9, **−2.8%**;
- code 24 188 bytes, static RAM 180 784, stack 564.

**Goldens made again,** moved only in time:
- fmgold: five of its seven sounds are identical to the sample; the other two diverge where an event moved one block;
- the MIDI out captures (midiout, midithru, midilocal, midiburst): the same bytes, shifted by −1.33 to +0.13 ms, except midiout, where two messages a block apart traded places;
- midiround's script, made again from midiout's capture.

> | The flash chip | 1 MiB. Erased (all `0xFF`) unless `--flash FILE` gives its first bytes. The image is then written into it at offset `0x4000`, as an installed image sits. Since 0.6.0 an erase or program takes time and keeps the chip busy ("The flash chip", below). |
55a56,99
> 
> ## The flash chip
> 
> Since 0.6.0 fwtest's flash chip behaves as the P25Q80H's datasheet says
> (`HARDWARE-SPEC.md`, HW-77, HW-78, HW-83), at its maximum times:
> 
> - **Busy times.** A page program keeps the chip busy for 3 ms and an
>   erase (a 256-byte page, 4 KiB, 32 KiB, 64 KiB or the whole chip) for
>   12 ms, from the moment chip select goes high. Meanwhile status register
>   1 reads bit 0 (busy) and bit 1 (write enable) set, and the chip ignores
>   every command but the status reads, the array and ID reads too.
> - **Command rules.** An erase or program needs the write enable command
>   first, or it is ignored. A program wraps within its 256-byte page and
>   only clears bits.
> - **The code window while busy.** While the chip is busy, a core that is
>   about to run code in the code window (the image, or the chip past it),
>   or reads it, ends the run as a fault: "ran code in the code window
>   while the flash chip was busy (an erase or program in progress)", or
>   "read the code window at ADDR while ...". That includes an interrupt
>   handler in the window, and core 1. So the code that erases or
>   programs, and waits, runs in RAM; so does any handler that can run
>   meanwhile, with everything it calls and reads; or interrupts stay
>   masked. fwtest checks only while the chip is busy: on the chip the
>   window is unavailable for the whole time the firmware works the flash
>   directly (HW-79), from its first command. Core 1 is checked on core
>   0's clock, which it trails by at most one run call (1024 instructions).
>   The audio output plays on through a busy time: it reads RAM.
> - **Persistence.** The chip lasts from one run to the next only through
>   files: `--flash FILE` starts a run from a saved chip (the image is
>   written at `0x4000` again), `--flash-out` saves it at the end, whatever
>   the outcome. Give one run's `flash.bin` to the next as `--flash`.
> - **A power cut.** `--power-cut MS` ends the run at MS (in place of
>   `--ms`) as if the power went then, and saves `flash.bin`. An erase or
>   program in progress keeps only the part done by then: its first bytes,
>   in address order, in proportion to the time gone (a 4 KiB erase cut a
>   quarter of the way through has its first 1 KiB erased and the rest as
>   before). That is fwtest's choice: on the chip an interrupted erase or
>   program leaves those bytes undefined, so a firmware must be able to
>   tell an interrupted write from a finished one (a check sum, or a marker
>   written last). `--flash-log` lists every erase and program with its
>   times, to aim a cut. A run that ends any other way (`--ms`, a halt, a
>   fault) during an erase or program saves `flash.bin` (with
>   `--flash-out`) as if that operation had finished: the bytes change when
>   it starts. Use `--power-cut` for a cut.

cd ~/Development/[REDACTED:private]/clean; export GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH=1; T=~/.claude/jobs/cd816ac2/tmp; TR=$(cat $T/trailer.txt); git switch -q -c m7/m8-proposal m7/store && cat > $T/c7.txt <<EOF
docs: M8's proposal: screens, controls, macros, presets, costs

What:    docs/M8-PROPOSAL.md, for the owner's review: the patch,
         operator/algorithm, envelope, settings and save screens (ASCII
         sketches, 40 columns), the controls per screen with SEL as
         shift, four macro knobs (BRIGHT, COLOR, SHAPE, MOTION), a bank of
         64 original presets in 8 categories and how they are made and
         tested, the live views' core and bus costs, and seven questions.
Why:     M7's prompt, part 2: M8 turns the engine into an instrument. A
         document only; nothing of M8 is built.
How:     from what the panel (HW-36) and the firmware already offer, and
         M2 to M7's measurements: a block 1.451 ms, 110 000 instructions
         loaded, a drawing budget of 4 352 ticks a block, at least 60.8 ms
         a whole frame on the chip's panel bus.
Result:  docs only; under ten minutes to read.
Sources: none
Exposure: firmware side, none (one FM-1-RE document on the stock
         firmware read, nothing used; EXPOSURE.md)
$TR
EOF
git add docs/M8-PROPOSAL.md && git commit -q -F $T/c7.txt && git push -q -u origin m7/m8-proposal 2>&1 | grep -v '^remote:'; cat > $T/pr4.md <<'EOF'
**What:** `docs/M8-PROPOSAL.md`, for the owner to review on a phone (about ten minutes). It covers:
- **the screens:** patch, operator/algorithm (the algorithm drawn with each operator's level live), envelope, settings, save, as ASCII sketches 40 columns wide;
- **the controls** per screen, with SEL as the shift key for the raised keys' second labels;
- **four macro knobs** as KNOB1 to KNOB4's default: BRIGHT, COLOR (harmonic to metallic), SHAPE (pluck to pad), MOTION;
- **presets:** a bank of 64 original presets, how they are made (from scratch in `tools/fm_patch.py`, never from anyone's factory sounds) and how they are tested;
- **costs:** core 0 and the panel's bus for the live views, from M2 to M7's measurements;
- **seven questions** for the owner.

**Why:** the M7 prompt, part 2. A document only; nothing of M8 is built.

**How:** from what the panel (HW-36) and the firmware already offer; no other hardware facts.

**Result:** docs only. The costs, in short:
- the live views take under 1% of core 0 on average, and each update fits one block's drawing budget;
- the panel's bus is the limit: both views at 30 updates a second take about 41% of it.

**Sources:** none

**Exposure:** firmware side, none to GPL material (EXPOSURE.md, #95). Model `claude-opus-5-5`.

**CI run:** this pull request's `ci` check.

**Record:** filled in after merge.

Stacked on #106: merge it after #106.

---
Merge (owner only): GitHub's "Create a merge commit" button, after CI passed on the head commit
(CONTRIBUTING.md, "Pull requests and merging").

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

https://claude.ai/code/session_011oy7nNZSEXzU6CiCVQe4K8
EOF
gh pr create --base main --head m7/m8-proposal --title "M8 proposal: screens, controls, macros, presets, costs" --body-file $T/pr4.md

-SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 japes98
-# M8 proposal: from engine to instrument
-A proposal for the owner to review, written at the end of M7. Nothing
-here is built yet. It uses only what the firmware and the panel already
-offer, and facts already in HARDWARE-SPEC.md. Decisions wanted are at
-the end.
-## What we start from
-- **Panel** (HW-36): a 240 x 240 colour screen; eight knobs (MASTER, a
-  pot; SELECT, PRESETS, ALGORITHM and KNOB1 to KNOB4, encoders with
-  detents); 14 buttons (OCT-, OCT+, FX, SEL, ENV, LFO, EDIT, GLO, HOME,
-  SAVE, ARP, SEQ, PLAY/STOP, REC), each with an LED; 27 keys, each with an
-  LED, ten raised keys carrying second labels: OP1 to OP6, PIT, GLO,
-  MONO, POLY.
-- **Engine** (M5 to M7): six operators, ten algorithms, 16 voices on two
-  cores, a pitch envelope, mono with glide, MIDI in and out, 9 test
-  patches, 16 user slots kept in flash.
-- **Today's controls:** PRESETS picks a program, ALGORITHM the algorithm,
-  KNOB1 to KNOB4 are pitch, glide, modulation depth and feedback; SEL
-  with MONO or POLY sets the mode; SAVE with a key saves.
-## Four rules
-1. **One screen at a time; HOME always goes back** to the patch view.
-2. **The bottom strip names what KNOB1 to KNOB4 do** on every screen,
-   with their values, so the knobs are never a guess.
-3. **Some knobs never change meaning:** MASTER is volume, PRESETS the
-   program, OCT- and OCT+ the octave, everywhere.
-4. **The screen shows the sound,** not only numbers: the algorithm
-   drawn with each operator's level moving as it plays, and a spectrum
-   of what comes out.
-## The screens
-### Patch view (HOME)
-| 012  GLASS BELL           POLY  O+0  |
-|  1>2 3>4   spectrum, live            |
-| BRIGHT  COLOR   SHAPE   MOTION       |
-The program and its name, the mode and octave; a small picture of the
-algorithm; the live spectrum. KNOB1 to KNOB4 are the four macros
-(below). ALGORITHM changes the algorithm, as now.
-### Operator and algorithm view (EDIT)
-| ALG 5            OP3 selected        |
-|   ##     #       ## = level now      |
-|  [3]==>[4]   (selected: double line) |
-| RATIO   LEVEL   DETUNE  VELO         |
-The algorithm drawn as boxes and arrows, carriers at the bottom. Under
-each box a bar shows that operator's level now (the loudest voice), so
-you see a modulator decay while the note sounds. SEL with OP1 to OP6
-picks the operator, whose key LED stays lit; KNOB1 to KNOB4 edit it.
-SELECT steps through the operator's other pages (mode and fixed
-frequency; the envelope's levels).
-### Envelope view (ENV)
-| ENV  OP3                  stage: D1  |
-| ATTACK  DECAY1  DECAY2  RELEASE      |
-The selected operator's envelope drawn to scale (time codes are
-logarithmic, so the drawing is too), and a dot where the last note is
-now. SELECT switches the knobs to the three levels. SEL with PIT shows
-the pitch envelope instead; SEL with GLO, the glide.
-### Settings (GLO)
-| SETTINGS                             |
-| > MIDI in channel     omni           |
-|   MIDI out channel    1              |
-|   Thru                off            |
-|   Local control       on             |
-|   Bend range          2              |
-|   Knobs               macros         |
-|   Store               5/16 used      |
-|   Factory reset       hold SAVE      |
-| SELECT: row    KNOB1: change         |
-Every setting in `struct midi_settings`, plus the knobs' mode (macros or
-the M5 controls) and the store's state. Changes are kept as M7 keeps
-them (2 s after the last change).
-### Save (SAVE)
-| SAVE  GLASS BELL  to slot:           |
-| SELECT: slot  SAVE: write  HOME: no  |
-M7's shortcut (SAVE held with a key) stays; the screen adds names, a
-slot picker and a confirmation before overwriting a slot in use.
-## The controls
-| Control | Everywhere | Patch | EDIT | ENV | Settings |
-| MASTER | volume | | | | |
-| PRESETS | program | | | | |
-| ALGORITHM | | algorithm | algorithm | | |
-| SELECT | | | operator page | rates / levels | row |
-| KNOB1-4 | | macros | operator | stage times | value (KNOB1) |
-| OCT- / OCT+ | octave | | | | |
-| HOME, EDIT, ENV, GLO, SAVE | go to that screen | | | | |
-| SEL + OP1-6 | | | pick operator | pick operator | |
-| SEL + PIT / GLO | | | | pitch env / glide | |
-| SEL + MONO / POLY | mode (as now) | | | | |
-| PLAY/STOP | audition note (the test tone today) | | | | |
-| FX, LFO, ARP, SEQ, REC | reserved for later milestones: the event line says so | | | | |
-SEL is the shift key: held, the raised keys do what their second label
-says and play no note. Keys without SEL always play. LEDs: the screen's
-button lit; the selected operator's key at half brightness; held keys
-fully lit, as now.
-## The four macros (KNOB1 to KNOB4 in the patch view)
-Each macro moves several of the patch's values at once, as an offset
-over the stored patch (as KNOB1 to KNOB4 do today), so turning it back
-returns the patch exactly. Each is sent and received as one MIDI
-controller (16 to 19, as now).
-- **BRIGHT** (brightness): every modulator's level up or down together,
-  so the index and the upper partials rise or fall. Today's KNOB3,
-  renamed.
-- **COLOR** (harmonic to metallic): the modulators' ratios move from
-  their whole-number values towards inharmonic ones (a fixed table of
-  targets per ratio, so the sweep is the same on every patch), and
-  feedback rises a little at the metallic end.
-- **SHAPE** (pluck to pad): the carriers' envelopes. At one end a fast
-  attack, a short decay and little sustain; at the other a slow attack,
-  full sustain and a long release. The middle is the patch as stored.
-- **MOTION:** vibrato depth, plus a small spread of detune across the
-  carriers, so a held note moves and widens.
-The M5 controls (pitch, glide, depth, feedback) stay available as a
-setting ("Knobs: direct"), for tests and for players who want them.
-## Presets: a bank of our own
-- **How many:** 64 presets in 8 categories of 8: keys, bass, bells and
-  mallets, brass and winds, pads, leads, plucks and strings, percussion
-  and effects. They sit in the image, after the 9 test patches; the 16
-  user slots stay as M7 made them.
-- **How they are made:** written from scratch in `tools/fm_patch.py`,
-  as the test patches are: ratios, levels and envelopes chosen by ear
-  and by reasoning (a bell's inharmonic ratios, a bass's short
-  modulator decay), each with a line saying what it is for. Never
-  derived from anyone's factory sounds: no voice banks or SysEx dumps are
-  opened, converted or compared, and no names are borrowed. Each preset's
-  history is its commits.
-- **How they are tested,** each one in fwtest, by a tool of our own:
-  - valid by `fm_patch.problems()`, and all 16 voices sounding within
-    the loaded budget;
-  - a reference note: no clipping, no DC, no click at note on or off,
-    loudness within 3 dB of a target, so the bank plays at one level;
-  - its category's shape: a bass has most of its energy below 300 Hz, a
-    pad no attack faster than 50 ms, a pluck decays by 30 dB within 2 s;
-  - a golden WAV of the reference note, so any change shows;
-  - and the owner listens before the bank is merged.
-## Costs
-From M5 to M7's measurements (fwtest): a block is 64 frames, 1.451 ms,
-about 348 000 core cycles at 240 MHz. Under the heaviest input, core 0
-spends about 110 000 instructions a block (32%), core 1 about 22%, and
-the screen may take at most 4 352 time base ticks a block, about 43 500
-instructions (12.5%). On the chip the panel's bus needs at least 60.8 ms
-for a whole frame (DESIGN-NOTES, M2), so live views redraw small regions,
-never the whole screen.
-| Live view | Core 0, each update | At 30 updates a second | Panel bus, at 30 a second |
-| Spectrum: 256-point real FFT of the output, 64 bars, 240 x 40 pixels | about 15 000 instructions (FFT with the float unit, window, magnitudes) | about 650 a block, 0.2% | 10.1 ms an update: 30% |
-| Algorithm: 6 level bars of 30 x 20 pixels | about 10 000 | about 430 a block, 0.1% | 3.8 ms an update: 11% |
-| Envelope dot | under 2 000 | under 100 a block | under 1% |

-# M8 proposal: from engine to instrument
-A proposal for the owner to review, written at the end of M7. Nothing
-here is built yet. It uses only what the firmware and the panel already
-offer, and facts already in HARDWARE-SPEC.md. Decisions wanted are at
-the end.
-## What we start from
-- **Panel** (HW-36): a 240 x 240 colour screen; eight knobs (MASTER, a
-  pot; SELECT, PRESETS, ALGORITHM and KNOB1 to KNOB4, encoders with
-  detents); 14 buttons (OCT-, OCT+, FX, SEL, ENV, LFO, EDIT, GLO, HOME,
-  SAVE, ARP, SEQ, PLAY/STOP, REC), each with an LED; 27 keys, each with an
-  LED, ten raised keys carrying second labels: OP1 to OP6, PIT, GLO,
-  MONO, POLY.
-- **Engine** (M5 to M7): six operators, ten algorithms, 16 voices on two
-  cores, a pitch envelope, mono with glide, MIDI in and out, 9 test
-  patches, 16 user slots kept in flash.
-- **Today's controls:** PRESETS picks a program, ALGORITHM the algorithm,
-  KNOB1 to KNOB4 are pitch, glide, modulation depth and feedback; SEL
-  with MONO or POLY sets the mode; SAVE with a key saves.
-## Four rules
-1. **One screen at a time; HOME always goes back** to the patch view.
-2. **The bottom strip names what KNOB1 to KNOB4 do** on every screen,
-   with their values, so the knobs are never a guess.
-3. **Some knobs never change meaning:** MASTER is volume, PRESETS the
-   program, OCT- and OCT+ the octave, everywhere.
-4. **The screen shows the sound,** not only numbers: the algorithm
-   drawn with each operator's level moving as it plays, and a spectrum
-   of what comes out.
-## The screens
-### Patch view (HOME)
-| 012  GLASS BELL           POLY  O+0  |
-|  1>2 3>4   spectrum, live            |
-| BRIGHT  COLOR   SHAPE   MOTION       |
-The program and its name, the mode and octave; a small picture of the
-algorithm; the live spectrum. KNOB1 to KNOB4 are the four macros
-(below). ALGORITHM changes the algorithm, as now.
-### Operator and algorithm view (EDIT)
-| ALG 5            OP3 selected        |
-|   ##     #       ## = level now      |
-|  [3]==>[4]   (selected: double line) |
-| RATIO   LEVEL   DETUNE  VELO         |
-The algorithm drawn as boxes and arrows, carriers at the bottom. Under
-each box a bar shows that operator's level now (the loudest voice), so
-you see a modulator decay while the note sounds. SEL with OP1 to OP6
-picks the operator, whose key LED stays lit; KNOB1 to KNOB4 edit it.
-SELECT steps through the operator's other pages (mode and fixed
-frequency; the envelope's levels).
-### Envelope view (ENV)
-| ENV  OP3                  stage: D1  |
-| ATTACK  DECAY1  DECAY2  RELEASE      |
-The selected operator's envelope drawn to scale (time codes are
-logarithmic, so the drawing is too), and a dot where the last note is
-now. SELECT switches the knobs to the three levels. SEL with PIT shows
-the pitch envelope instead; SEL with GLO, the glide.
-### Settings (GLO)
-| SETTINGS                             |
-| > MIDI in channel     omni           |
-|   MIDI out channel    1              |
-|   Thru                off            |
-|   Local control       on             |
-|   Bend range          2              |
-|   Knobs               macros         |
-|   Store               5/16 used      |
-|   Factory reset       hold SAVE      |
-| SELECT: row    KNOB1: change         |
-Every setting in `struct midi_settings`, plus the knobs' mode (macros or
-the M5 controls) and the store's state. Changes are kept as M7 keeps
-them (2 s after the last change).
-### Save (SAVE)
-| SAVE  GLASS BELL  to slot:           |
-| SELECT: slot  SAVE: write  HOME: no  |
-M7's shortcut (SAVE held with a key) stays; the screen adds names, a
-slot picker and a confirmation before overwriting a slot in use.
-## The controls
-| Control | Everywhere | Patch | EDIT | ENV | Settings |
-| MASTER | volume | | | | |
-| PRESETS | program | | | | |
-| ALGORITHM | | algorithm | algorithm | | |
-| SELECT | | | operator page | rates / levels | row |
-| KNOB1-4 | | macros | operator | stage times | value (KNOB1) |
-| OCT- / OCT+ | octave | | | | |
-| HOME, EDIT, ENV, GLO, SAVE | go to that screen | | | | |
-| SEL + OP1-6 | | | pick operator | pick operator | |
-| SEL + PIT / GLO | | | | pitch env / glide | |
-| SEL + MONO / POLY | mode (as now) | | | | |
-| PLAY/STOP | audition note (the test tone today) | | | | |
-| FX, LFO, ARP, SEQ, REC | reserved for later milestones: the event line says so | | | | |
-SEL is the shift key: held, the raised keys do what their second label
-says and play no note. Keys without SEL always play. LEDs: the screen's
-button lit; the selected operator's key at half brightness; held keys
-fully lit, as now.
-## The four macros (KNOB1 to KNOB4 in the patch view)
-Each macro moves several of the patch's values at once, as an offset
-over the stored patch (as KNOB1 to KNOB4 do today), so turning it back
-returns the patch exactly. Each is sent and received as one MIDI
-controller (16 to 19, as now).
-- **BRIGHT** (brightness): every modulator's level up or down together,
-  so the index and the upper partials rise or fall. Today's KNOB3,
-  renamed.
-- **COLOR** (harmonic to metallic): the modulators' ratios move from
-  their whole-number values towards inharmonic ones (a fixed table of
-  targets per ratio, so the sweep is the same on every patch), and
-  feedback rises a little at the metallic end.
-- **SHAPE** (pluck to pad): the carriers' envelopes. At one end a fast
-  attack, a short decay and little sustain; at the other a slow attack,
-  full sustain and a long release. The middle is the patch as stored.
-- **MOTION:** vibrato depth, plus a small spread of detune across the
-  carriers, so a held note moves and widens.
-The M5 controls (pitch, glide, depth, feedback) stay available as a
-setting ("Knobs: direct"), for tests and for players who want them.
-## Presets: a bank of our own
-- **How many:** 64 presets in 8 categories of 8: keys, bass, bells and
-  mallets, brass and winds, pads, leads, plucks and strings, percussion
-  and effects. They sit in the image, after the 9 test patches; the 16
-  user slots stay as M7 made them.
-- **How they are made:** written from scratch in `tools/fm_patch.py`,
-  as the test patches are: ratios, levels and envelopes chosen by ear
-  and by reasoning (a bell's inharmonic ratios, a bass's short
-  modulator decay), each with a line saying what it is for. Never
-  derived from anyone's factory sounds: no voice banks or SysEx dumps are
-  opened, converted or compared, and no names are borrowed. Each preset's
-  history is its commits.
-- **How they are tested,** each one in fwtest, by a tool of our own:
-  - valid by `fm_patch.problems()`, and all 16 voices sounding within
-    the loaded budget;
-  - a reference note: no clipping, no DC, no click at note on or off,
-    loudness within 3 dB of a target, so the bank plays at one level;
-  - its category's shape: a bass has most of its energy below 300 Hz, a
-    pad no attack faster than 50 ms, a pluck decays by 30 dB within 2 s;
-  - a golden WAV of the reference note, so any change shows;
-  - and the owner listens before the bank is merged.
-## Costs
-From M5 to M7's measurements (fwtest): a block is 64 frames, 1.451 ms,
-about 348 000 core cycles at 240 MHz. Under the heaviest input, core 0
-spends about 110 000 instructions a block (32%), core 1 about 22%, and
-the screen may take at most 4 352 time base ticks a block, about 43 500
-instructions (12.5%). On the chip the panel's bus needs at least 60.8 ms
-for a whole frame (DESIGN-NOTES, M2), so live views redraw small regions,
-never the whole screen.
-| Live view | Core 0, each update | At 30 updates a second | Panel bus, at 30 a second |
-| Spectrum: 256-point real FFT of the output, 64 bars, 240 x 40 pixels | about 15 000 instructions (FFT with the float unit, window, magnitudes) | about 650 a block, 0.2% | 10.1 ms an update: 30% |
-| Algorithm: 6 level bars of 30 x 20 pixels | about 10 000 | about 430 a block, 0.1% | 3.8 ms an update: 11% |
-| Envelope dot | under 2 000 | under 100 a block | under 1% |
-So the live views together cost under 1% of core 0 on average, and each
-update fits in one block's drawing budget. The bus is the limit: both
-live views at 30 updates a second take about 41% of it (at 20, about
-28%), which leaves room for the knobs' 16 ms frames. The proposal: 30
-updates a second on the patch view's spectrum alone, 20 when the
-algorithm's bars show too. RAM: about 2 KiB for the FFT's buffers
-(the output's last 256 samples, copied by the engine each block). The
-engine adds one small record for the views: each operator's loudest
-level, written once a block. Nothing moves to core 1.
-## Questions for the owner
-1. **Buttons:** HW-36 lists 14 buttons (OCT- and OCT+ included); the
-   prompt said twelve. The table uses all 14. Right?
-2. **Shift key:** SEL as shift (it already is with MONO and POLY), or
-   hold the screen's own button?
-3. **Macros on save:** stay offsets (the saved patch is the stored one;
-   the macros come back to zero), or be written into the patch on SAVE?
-4. **Sizes:** 64 presets and 16 user slots? More user slots (64, say)
-   need the store's next format, since their records would outgrow one
-   sector.
-5. **Spectrum:** on the patch view by default? Log or linear frequency?
-6. **Factory reset:** keep M7's hold of SAVE and HOME, or move it into
-   Settings with a confirmation?
-7. **Reserved buttons** (FX, LFO, ARP, SEQ, REC): which comes next after

input.content:
---
name: ci-artifacts-named-files
description: Clean side: a CI report artifact downloaded whole carries the record's harness/ folder; take named files only, and how to find a C-SEP-TERMS hit
metadata:
  type: feedback
---

A `gh run download` of a CI report artifact brings the whole record, including its `harness/` folder of harness test results. M7 (2026-10-24) did that twice, opened only named logs, deleted both and recorded it in EXPOSURE.md.

**Why:** the clean-room rules let clean sessions take only named files of the firmware's own records; a whole artifact is the record wholesale.

**How to apply:**
- Read CI results from `gh run view <id> --log` first.
- If an artifact file is needed, name the file, or delete the artifact at once and record it.
- C-SEP-TERMS gives only a place and a hash (`sha256(word)[:16]`). Hash the flagged line's words the same way to find the word.
- A false positive goes in `config/emulator-terms-reviewed.json` by its own PR, which keeps a budget PR clean.

Related: [[provenance-ids-race]]

---
name: ci-artifacts-named-files
description: Clean side: a CI report artifact downloaded whole carries the record's harness/ folder; take named files only, and how to find a C-SEP-TERMS hit
metadata:
  type: feedback
---

A `gh run download` of a CI report artifact brings the whole record, including its `harness/` folder of harness test results. M7 (2026-10-24) did that twice, opened only named logs, deleted both and recorded it in EXPOSURE.md.

**Why:** the clean-room rules let clean sessions take only named files of the firmware's own records; a whole artifact is the record wholesale.

**How to apply:**
- Read CI results from `gh run view <id> --log` first.
- If an artifact file is needed, name the file, or delete the artifact at once and record it.
- C-SEP-TERMS gives only a place and a hash (`sha256(word)[:16]`). Hash the flagged line's words the same way to find the word.
- A false positive goes in `config/emulator-terms-reviewed.json` by its own PR, which keeps a budget PR clean.

Related: [[provenance-ids-race]]

content.text:
I finished M7 and the M8 proposal. All work is in six stacked pull requests, nothing is merged, and no releases or tags were made. The store is fully tested in fwtest, but the build has not been on a real FM-1, and it isn't safe to try there yet (Q-22 below).

done, ready to clear

## Questions (my reading meanwhile in brackets)
1. **A storage document I read.** FM-1-RE's `docs/io/09-storage.md` is on CONTRIBUTING's allowed list, and the spec side cites it (P-9). Most of it turned out to describe the stock firmware's own code, which CONTRIBUTING forbids. I read it once and deleted my copy, and I use nothing from it. My store design was written in the transcript before I opened it, and it differs from what the document describes. Does this change my role? *(Recorded in EXPOSURE.md; I kept working as firmware side.)*
2. **Where the store lives.** It uses `0xEA000`–`0xFBFFF`, the region where the stock firmware keeps its own user patches. On a unit that has stock patches, our firmware would erase them. Acceptable? *(Kept in one definition so it is easy to move.)*
3. **Q-22, not for real hardware yet.** The driver uses PD0 as the flash's chip select, as fwtest does. On the chip, PD0 may be the flash's clock. The JEDEC ID check blocks writes to an unknown part, but the start-up reads still happen. *(Treat the drop build as fwtest-only.)*
4. **Knobs and saving.** KNOB1–4 stay offsets and are not saved with a patch; saving keeps only the algorithm and the mode. *(Avoids applying the knobs twice; M8 settles it.)*
5. **Budgets.** Stack budget 768 bytes (measured 564), code 28,672 bytes, static RAM 196,608 bytes in #98. OK?
6. **Buttons.** The prompt says twelve, but HW-36 lists 14 (OCT- and OCT+ included). *(The M8 proposal uses all 14.)*
7. **fwtest 0.6.0 (#99).** It has no pin PR yet, so I didn't use it. I expect the store tests to pass on it, but haven't run them. *(Merge #106 first, then re-run CI after the pin.)*

## Merge order
**#95 → #96 → #97 → #108 → #98 → #106 → #107**
- **#95:** session start and spec request SR-9. CI passes.
- **#96, #97:** the spec side's. #97 is SR-9's answer and already contains #95's commits unchanged.
- **#108:** marks `ram_code`, my name for the code that runs from RAM, as a known false positive. The word also appears in the emulator's source, so the check that looks for such words (C-SEP-TERMS) fails #98, #106 and #107 until #108 is merged. Merge it, then re-run CI on #98, #106 and #107. CI passes.
- **#98:** budgets only.
- **#106:** the store. Every other check passes in CI, including the firmware suite (189 s with the store cases).
- **#107:** the M8 proposal, `docs/M8-PROPOSAL.md`.

#106 will conflict with #97 in two files; keep both sides in each:
- **`PROVENANCE.md`:** #97's P-51 to P-53, then P-54.
- **`docs/EXPOSURE.md`:** the M7 entry's "Later in the session" bullets, then #97's entry.

**REVIEWED.json** (approved by merging #95): M6b's `toolu_01XRtz1Dn5SmZEMvk974d8Zf` and `toolu_01Vr1WDihFeroeqf5ciRv2v7`. Both name a spec-side folder only as an excluded path. The next session's transcript check will also flag a few of my commands for the same reason (the folder names appear only to exclude them).

## M7 results
- **Code runs from RAM.** Everything except the 120-byte boot code is copied to RAM at start-up, because nothing may read the flash's code window while an erase or program is running (HW-79).
- **The store.** It keeps 16 user slots, the patch selection and the MIDI settings, migrating version 1 settings to version 2. Records are only ever appended and each carries a checksum, so a power cut leaves the previous copy readable. Sectors are reused in turn to spread wear. At 100,000 erase cycles, the selection and settings both changing every 2 s nonstop would last about 2.3 years.
- **Panel.** Hold SAVE and press one of the 16 leftmost keys to save the current patch to that slot. Hold SAVE and HOME for 2 s to restore factory defaults. The screen says what happened.
- **Power-cut test.** One save was cut at 109 points: after each of its 28 flash commands, and part way through every write. 29 more half-written images were made in Python. Every image held the old or the new patch with nothing else changed, and the firmware started from each and saved again.
- **Other tests:** the screen messages (checked against reference images), a damaged store, a full store (save refused, nothing written), migration, and wear.
- **Saving never interrupted audio.** On audioload's input with 24 saves, there were no audio underruns, including on a build using the flash part's longest erase and write times and on one that erased its own code from flash.
- **Speed and size.** Steady state +0.7%, loaded −2.8%, code 24,188 bytes, static RAM 180,784 bytes, stack 564 bytes.
- **Re-recorded test outputs.** The copy at start-up shifts timing slightly, so fmgold and four MIDI captures were re-recorded. Each was checked first: the same notes and bytes, only shifted in time.
- **Drop build:** `~/Development/<top>/drop/small-beeps-eb0d82d.bin`, SHA-256 `2d17f994b093f06ea171b16beedcf3182eaf5ba87017bdba8016e6e67659af44`, the same as CI's build. PLAN.md records M7 and names M8 next.

Free disk is about 3 GB. The clean-folder check found nothing spec-side on disk or in `.git`.
